title.en: The Mantis's Magic: Hartebeest Charm for Babies
title.zh: 螳螂之法：護嬰之麋羚符

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1874 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §13a; D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Hartebeest and the Eland'

summary.en: The Hartebeest and the Eland are things of the Mantis and have magic power: the hartebeest's head resembles his head. A mother with a young child must not eat hartebeest nor spring over its head, or the Mantis would press in the hollow of the child's head; she cuts a piece of hartebeest foot into a charm. When a man shoots an eland he stays away, ill, so the eland may smell no cooking.
summary.zh: 麋羚與大羚乃螳螂之物，具魔力：麋羚之頭似其頭。抱嬰之母不得食麋羚、不得跨其頭，否則螳螂壓陷兒之囟門；她截麋羚足一塊為符。射羚之獵者離家如病，使羚不嗅炊香。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San charm-lore from the Bleek & Lloyd archive (L V.—6. 4411-4434) and D. F. Bleek 1924; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Hartebeest and the Eland are things of the Mantis; therefore they have magic power. The Mantis is used to go with the Hartebeest when he walks about. Our parents used to ask us, Did we not see that the Hartebeest's head resembled the Mantis's head? It feels that it belongs to the Mantis: that is why its head resembles his head.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 10 (public domain).

passages.text: A woman who has a young child does not eat the Hartebeest, nor does she spring over the Hartebeest's head, for the Mantis would press down the hollow place on her child's head, and the child would die, if she did so. So our parents used to tell the women who had young children to cut out a piece of the Hartebeest's foot between the toes, to thread it upon a sinew and make a charm and put it on the little child.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 10 (public domain).

passages.text: When a man has shot an Eland with an arrow, he does not come home. He walks about as if he were ill; people carry him away as if he were ill, for he wants the Eland to act as he does... he goes to a place to windward, so that he may not smell the food the people are cooking at home. For if the Eland were to smell the scent of the food, it would arise and go away.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 10-11 (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's 1875 note (§13a): an account of the magic protection afforded by the Mantis to the Hartebeest and to the Eland, dictated in the Katkop dialect by Dia!kwain; the same informant mentions remarkable superstitions concerning the Hartebeest, whose head is said to resemble that of the Mantis, and a curious charm made from the foot of the Hartebeest, used by Bushman women for their children.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §13a; not verbatim.

title.en: How the Mantis Gave the Bucks Their Colours

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'How the Mantis gave the Bucks their Colours'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §1

summary.en: The Gemsbok ate white liquid honey and is white; the Hartebeest ate the red comb of young bees and is red; the Eland ate wasps' honey and is dark; the Quagga ate small bees' honey and is dark; the Springbok drank the liquid from the red young bees' cells and is red. The Mantis squeezed each out for its animal.
summary.zh: 大羚食白蜜故白；麋羚食紅嫩蜂巢故赤；伊蘭羚食黃蜂蜜故暗；斑馬食小蜂蜜故暗；跳羚飲紅巢之液故赤。皆螳螂為之榨取。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San etiology from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Gemsbok once ate liquid honey which is white. This is why he is white. The Mantis once gave some of it to the Gemsbok. The Hartebeest was the one to whom the Mantis once gave some of the comb of young bees; that is why the Hartebeest is red, because the comb of young bees which he ate was red. So he became like the comb of young bees.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 10 (public domain).

passages.text: The Eland was the one to whom the Mantis once gave some wasps honey; this is why he is dark, because he once ate wasps honey. The Quagga was the one to whom the Mantis once gave some of the small bees' honey; that is why he is dark... The Springbok was the one who once ate the liquid from the young bees' cells; that is why he is red. The Mantis squeezed it out for him and he drank.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 10 (public domain).

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Mantis and the Will-o'-the-Wisp'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §4

summary.en: The Mantis meets a smooth-headed being whose eyes are not in his head but between the toes of his feet; beaten the first time, he consults the Ichneumon, and the second time kicks dust into the eyes on his feet and breaks the will-o'-the-wisp's head.
summary.zh: 螳螂遇頭頂平滑之怪——其目不在首而在趾間。初戰敗北，商於小獴；再戰以塵揚其足間之眼，碎鬼火之頭。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Mantis caught sight of Will-o'-the-wisp walking about; he asked where Will-o'-the-wisp came from... he put down his quiver, he took out a knobkerry, he looked to see where Will-o'-the-wisp's eyes were. He looked him up and down, he walked all round him seeking his eyes. He asked Will-o'-the-wisp where his eyes might be. Will-o'-the-wisp said that his eyes were not anywhere.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 13 (public domain).

passages.text: And Will-o'-the-wisp hit the Mantis's head and broke it, and hit it again. And the Mantis sprang aside and ran away, because he felt he could not bear it any longer. Then he called to the quiver and the shoes, that his things should follow him home.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 14 (public domain).

passages.text: Kwammang-a told him that Will-o'-the-wisp's eyes ought to be on his feet between the great toe and the next... 'Then you must look at his feet and you will see the eyes peeping out between the toes. Then you must kick dust into his eyes, and while he sits rubbing his eyes there, you must keep hitting his head.'... And the Mantis sprang up and beat his head and broke it.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 14-15 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: A Visit to the Lion's House

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'A Visit to the Lion's House'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §5

summary.en: Kwammang-a and the Ichneumon visit the lions' home to eat quagga meat; the Mantis begs to come, hides in the bag, and whispers 'I should like to poke out your eye' to the little Lion, who runs crying to the Lioness. She stamps to crush him; the Mantis flies off with his calling shoes, then lies to the Dasse that both men were slain — until the Porcupine sees them coming laden.
summary.zh: 夸曼加與小獴訪獅家食斑馬肉；螳螂強要同行，藏於囊中，對小獅耳語「欲挖爾眼」。小獅啼告母獅；母獅欲踏殺之，螳螂展翅而遁，沿路呼其鞋。歸家謊報二人已死——豪豬卻見其滿載而歸。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Mantis said: 'O Ichneumon, put me into your bag!'... 'Quickly put me in, O Ichneumon, quickly put me in, so that the Lions do not see me! You must put in my legs, you must not tie up the mouth of the bag, for my head will stand above the bag's mouth... Just then the little Lion came in among Kwammang-a's people. The little Lion caught sight of him.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 16 (public domain).

passages.text: The little Lion sprang back crying... As he stood by Kwammang-a's leg, he saw the Mantis. The Mantis shut one eye and winked at him, he whispered: 'I should like to poke out your eye.' The little Lion ran away crying; he went to his mother... She stood upon the Mantis to crush him. She said: 'Boo, what is this that is making the child cry, bringing me, the Lioness?' Then the Mantis jumped out of the bag and got feathers; he flew up into the sky.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 16 (public domain).

passages.text: He went into the water... He stood on the bank above and said: 'O Hartebeest's children: wait for me!' O shoes, wait for me! O stick, wait for me! O bow, wait for me!... The Hartebeest-skin bag said: 'That man... now he speaks thus.' The shoes said: 'Let us go away and leave him... he is mocking us, he is deceiving us.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 17-18 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: He sat down and said: 'O Dasse, we went to the Lion's house; the Lion slew Kwammang-a. He cheated the Dasse, he deceived her, because he is a liar. He also said: The Lion has swallowed the Ichneumon.'... The Porcupine got up and went out. She saw Kwammang-a's party coming laden with Quagga's meat... The Porcupine said: 'You sat there telling lies.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 18 (public domain).

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Mantis and the Cat'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §6

summary.en: The Mantis attacks the Cat who sings of the Lynx's mockery; the cat buries its head in the ground and the Mantis can only strike its tail. The Ichneumon teaches him: feint at the head, watch where it hides, then strike breaking it — and the Mantis breaks the cat's head, boasting 'What man is our equal?'
summary.zh: 貓歌其為獰貓所嘲；螳螂攻之，貓首埋地，螳螂唯擊其尾。小獴教之：佯攻其首，觀其藏處，再擊碎之。螳螂破貓首，自詡「何人堪比吾儕？」

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: He met the Cat going along singing. The Cat sang that the Lynx mocked at him, because he could not run as fast as the Lynx did... The Cat said: 'Your eyes have warts on them. I will hit your head, I will break it.' The Mantis said: 'O Cat, hit my head, I will hit your head!'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 19 (public domain).

passages.text: The Mantis struck at the Cat's head; the Cat drew back and hid his head in the ground. The Mantis hit the Cat's tail... The Cat hit the Mantis's head and broke it. The Mantis quickly got feathers, he flew away. He called to the Hartebeest-skin bag: 'O Hartebeest's children, leave here, we must fly.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 19 (public domain).

passages.text: The Ichneumon said: 'O Mantis, we always feint at the Cat's head, the Cat hides his head in the ground, we look to see where his head is, we strike, breaking it.'... He feinted at the Cat's head. The Cat quickly put his head into the ground, thinking that the Mantis would strike his tail again. The Mantis saw his head just above the ground; he struck at it and hit it.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 20-21 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: The Mantis and the Proteles: Roasted on His Own Fire
title.zh: 螳螂與土狼：自焚於己火

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Mantis and the Proteles'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §8

summary.en: Kwammang-a begs a lean little Proteles from his aunt's hole; the Mantis, greedy, goes back alone for another. The mother grips him with one arm and the little Proteles with the other and knocks him down on the fire he had made; he springs up crying 'O blisters!', flies to the water, and comes home moaning.
summary.zh: 夸曼加自姨母洞中求得小土狼一隻；螳螂貪心獨返再求。母土狼一臂抱幼獸、一臂擒螳螂，將其擲於自燃之火上。螳螂呼「燙泡矣！」，飛至水邊，歸家呻吟。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Kwammang-a said: 'O my Aunt! Come out and give me one, that I may put it to roast for myself.' Then the Mother Proteles came out... Then Kwammang-a said: 'I have begged you to give me one, that I may rub off the dust, for you see I am white with dust.' And the Mother Proteles said: 'O man, my children are not grown up yet, they are still little.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 21-22 (public domain).

passages.text: The Mantis was greedy; therefore he turned back to the Proteles... He said: 'O my Aunt, come out, give me a little thing to cut up, that I may rub off the dust from myself.' Then the Proteles stuck out her head while her body was inside... she went in and took a little girl Proteles and pulled her out.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 22 (public domain).

passages.text: Then the Proteles caught hold of the Mantis with one arm, she pulled the Mantis on to the fire, while she kept fast hold of the little Proteles. She knocked the Mantis down on the fire which he had shewn her. Then the Mantis said: 'O blisters! Hartebeest's children, you must go'... He descended when he saw the water was near... he popped into the water.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 22-23 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: Foulmouth, the Blue Crane and the Girls

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'Foulmouth, the Blue Crane and the Girls'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §35a

summary.en: Foulmouth lies on an umbrella-top tree over the girls digging ants' eggs; the Blue Crane — Kaggen's sister — hiccough-hating, shields each girl with her own body, is stabbed, cut shoulder from shoulder and head from neck, and joins herself together again crying 'O Foulmouth, I am coming!' until, huts near, he flees.
summary.zh: 穢口獸臥於傘頂樹上，窺掘蟻卵之少女。藍鶴——卡根之姊——以身蔽各女，屢被刺；肩斷復續，首斷復續，呼「穢口，吾至矣！」直至茅屋相近，獸遁。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San tale from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; contains violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Foulmouth is a person; he was a man of the early race. The Blue Crane was also a person of the early race. She was the Mantis's elder sister. The girls were girls of the early race... One old woman used always to go out with the girls... Foulmouth lay upon an umbrella-top tree. The girls went to sit in the shade of the tree, for they wanted to sift ants' eggs.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 23 (public domain).

passages.text: Then Foulmouth hiccoughed, and the Blue Crane exclaimed: 'Humph, humph! Abominable! What decayed thing can be smelling here?' The girls were silent, because they saw Foulmouth up the tree... Then Foulmouth climbed down the tree while she was walking along. Then Foulmouth ran on past the Blue Crane.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 24 (public domain).

passages.text: She covered the girl with her own body, and Foulmouth stabbed her. She lay as if dying upon her back... She arose behind Foulmouth's back... and she covered the girl. Foulmouth stabbed her back... Foulmouth grew angry and cut her. He cut off her shoulder and hurled it away... Her shoulders joined on again, she exclaimed: 'O Foulmouth! I am coming! I am coming!...'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 24-25 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: The Blue Crane rose up, she walked after him, she exclaimed: 'O Foulmouth, stab my heart!' Foulmouth walked on, for he felt angry. The Blue Crane said: 'O Foulmouth, stab me!... Then give me the spear and I will stab you.' Foulmouth snatched the spear away, when the Blue Crane caught at it in order to stab him... and she turned back and went home, while he went away.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 25 (public domain).

title.en: The Blue Crane's Story: The Merrythought and the Two Star-Lions
title.zh: 藍鶴之故事：願骨與雙星獅

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Blue Crane's Story'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §26

summary.en: The Frog's husband sulks, flees into a stone at a beetle's flight, and the Blue Crane hunts his spoor till grief turns her to bones. Two lions — 'Belt' and 'Mat', now the Pointers to the Southern Cross — eat her; her merrythought springs from Belt's mouth. The Mantis finds it, sets it in the water, and she grows again; he clothes her, anoints her with his scent, and brings her home as his sister.
summary.zh: 蛙夫鬱而遁入石中；藍鶴尋其跡，悲瘦成骨。二獅「貝爾」與「馬特」——今南十字導星——食之；其願骨自獅口躍出。螳螂拾之，置於水中，鶴復生；為之製衣，以己汗塗面認親，攜之歸家。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San myth from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

narrative.en:
The Blue Crane's friend was the Frog. The Frog's husband sat and sulked because his wife would not speak to him; a beetle flew past his nose and he jumped up and ran into a flat stone. The Blue Crane searched for his spoor to catch him for her friend, and missed him; she grew lean with grief, she became bones.

The Lions heard her searching — two lions called 'Belt' and 'Mat', who are now the stars, the pointers to the Southern Cross. They stole up, killed and ate her. 'Mat' said: 'O Belt, I do not want this person's bone to spring out of your mouth'; and while they ate, the Blue Crane's merrythought sprang out of Belt's mouth and lay nearby. They could not find it and went away.

The Mantis sought his sister. He followed the lions' spoor to the killing-place and found the merrythought, which was big. He put it into the water and went home. When he returned, the Blue Crane jumped up and splashed into the water; he left her in peace. Again and again he came, saw her growing in the sun — she had grown — and turned back without startling her, and made clothes for her meanwhile. When she seemed a grown girl, he stole up, caught her as she tried to reach the water, rubbed her face with his perspiration, and said: 'It is I, the Tinderbox, your elder brother; leave off struggling and sit down.' He put the cap, kaross and skin petticoat on her, and took her home.

The myth knits three threads: the resurrection-by-water that also revives the ostrich feather and the Moon; the star-names of the two lions, who stand silent forever near their lionesses; and the Mantis's strange double role as sister-seeker and scent-anointing father. The myth is tied to the stars: 'Belt' and 'Mat' are the two male lions that stand as the Pointers to the Southern Cross, and the lionesses that sit silent near them are Alpha, Beta and Gamma Crucis; one of the lions became a star because a girl looked at him, and the other followed. In the longer version the kori bustard \gi and her child escape while the Blue Crane is eaten, and the surviving bird is pulled up by the Crow to a thorn-tree, where heated stones are made ready; the pursuing lion is drawn up with a rope of mouse's entrails, breaks it, and falls into the fire and is roasted; then the greedy lion swallows a male tortoise whole, and the tortoise curses every pool dry and warns all game away until he starves. The Mantis's recovery of his sister is therefore the quiet ending of a great star-myth: grief that turns the searcher to bones, the merrythought that springs from the eater's mouth, and the water that grows her again into the sister the Tinderbox clothes and carries home.

functions: Accounts for the Pointer stars of the Southern Cross as once-living lions.
Extends the resurrection-by-water complex to a bird of the early race.
Models kinship recognition by scent in Bushman social thought.

variants.name: Pointer-lions expanded version (§26, L II.—1/2)
variants.summary: A longer version in which the kori bustard \gi and her child escape while the Blue Crane is eaten, and the surviving bird drops the lion into a fire of heated stones.

passages.text: The Blue Crane's friend was the Frog. The Frog was a person; her husband was a person; the Blue Crane was a person. They were people of the early race. The Frog's husband sat and sulked, because the Frog would not speak to him. And as he sat there, the Beetle came flying; the Beetle flew past his nose, and he jumped up, he ran away... he went into a stone, a flat stone.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 26 (public domain).

passages.text: And she grew lean, while she was searching there. Grief made her grow lean; she became bones. And the Lions heard her as she was searching there, two Lions: 'Belt' and 'Mat'. The Lions followed the sound to her... The Lions killed her and ate her... The Blue Crane's merrythought sprang out of 'Belt's' mouth and went and lay nearby. They tried to find it, but they could not see it, so they went away.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 26-27 (public domain). [These lions are now stars, the pointers to the Southern Cross. — D. F. Bleek's note]

passages.text: Then the Mantis sought the Blue Crane... he caught sight of the merrythought lying there, for it was big. He picked it up and went and put it into the water... The Blue Crane jumped up and splashed into the water... Once more he went out to look. As he came up, he saw the Blue Crane sitting in the sun. She had grown. He turned back without startling her... he went to make things, clothes which he meant to give to the Blue Crane, when she grew up.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 27 (public domain).

passages.text: He caught hold of her; when she tried to get into the water, he held her fast and rubbed her face with his perspiration; he made her smell his scent. He told the Blue Crane that he was her brother. It was he, the 'Tinderbox', who was holding her... Then the Blue Crane sat down. He covered her with a cap which he had made for her, and with a kaross and a skin petticoat... Then he took the Blue Crane with him; they returned home.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 28 (public domain).

title.en: The Mantis and the Magic Bird's Eggs

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Mantis and the Magic Bird'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §9

summary.en: The Mantis robs the talking ostrich — the Magic Bird — whose eggs and brush-spoon stick to his mouth and whose load sticks to his back; he must carry them home until daybreak, when all falls off. Warned by the Ichneumon, he next takes only the little outside egg, then robs a real ostrich safely.
summary.zh: 螳螂劫會言之鴕——魔鳥；其卵與匙黏於其口，負荷黏於其背，直至天明方落。小獴戒之，此後只取巢外小卵；再向真鴕取卵，則安然無恙。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Mantis went out at daybreak. As he went he saw the Magic Bird sitting on her eggs. He shot at her; the arrow returned; the Mantis dodged it and said: 'Is this an Ostrich? She does not run away.' The Magic Bird said to the Mantis: 'You may take the little egg standing outside there and drink it.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 28 (public domain).

passages.text: He put the brush to his mouth. He pulled out his tongue with it and said: 'Is this an Ostrich? It is pulling out my tongue. My tongue is sticking to the brush.'... He took the yolk, he was silent, for the brush was in his mouth... He carried the eggs in the net. He returned home with an egg sticking to his mouth and the net sticking fast behind his back.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 28-29 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: The Ichneumon said to him: 'O Mantis, you must be carrying the Magic Bird's eggs! We always go and take the Magic Bird's little outside eggs... The Magic Bird talks, an Ostrich does not talk, for the Ostrich is afraid of us. The Magic Bird talks, because she is a different kind of Ostrich, the kind of Ostrich which talks.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 29 (public domain).

passages.text: Then he grew nervous. He hoped that the brush would not stick fast... He put the brush away in the bag, he took the quiver and slung it on... He walked away, he went up to a real Ostrich... He felt that his hands were not sticking fast. He said to himself: 'Ah, I must have been mistaken...' Then he picked up the eggs, he loaded up quickly... He trotted quickly away.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 29-30 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: The Mantis Takes Away the Ticks' Sheep

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Mantis takes away the Ticks' Sheep'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §10

summary.en: The black, bloody-handed Ticks hide in their sheep's wool and drop one by one on the visiting Mantis, beating him nearly to death. He flies to the water, dreams, and steals their whole kraal up into the sky: the sheep, houses, pots and knobkerries descend beside his own. Fireless, the Ticks must henceforth bite and suck blood raw.
summary.zh: 黑膚血手之蜱人藏於羊毛中，逐一落擊來訪之螳螂，幾斃之。他飛至水邊，夢而復仇：將其全欄羊群、屋舍、釜甑、棍棒自天而降置於己旁。蜱人失火，自茲惟有生啜血。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: They saw him; they said to each other: 'What man comes yonder?'... 'We will creep into the sheep's wool, that he may come to the house. This little child must stay; he shall look after the pots on the fire...' The Mantis walked up to the child. 'Am I like a fighting man, that the people have gone away in fear...?' The people listened in the sheep's wool.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 30 (public domain).

passages.text: A big young man Tick slipped down beside the Mantis; he sat holding the Mantis by the kaross. His other brother slipped down on the other side of the Mantis... Their father was still above, an old Tick... 'The Mantis slipped out of the kaross. The Ticks rushed together and struck at him... He went away first, his things followed him.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 30-31 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: The Mantis sat down... he said: 'The people to whom I went must have been hidden, for I did not see them. They kept coming out from above, they kept sliding down... while the sheep were in the kraal.' The Ichneumon said: 'You went to the house to which people do not go... For those people are black; they are wont to beat a man to death because of those sheep.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 31-32 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: The sheep rise up, the sheep come and stand in front of his house... The sheep came out of the sky, they stood; the things also came out of the sky and sat down, while the people slept there... 'It seemed right to me, because those people attacked me... They shall now drink raw blood because they lack a fire... The old Tick shall always stand biting men's skins, he shall suck out blood, for he altogether lacks a knife.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 32-34 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: The All-Devourer: Swallowed and Cut Out Again

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Mantis and the All-devourer'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §10-11

summary.en: To punish the Ticks the Mantis summons |Khwa-hemm, the All-devourer — the Porcupine's real father, whose tongue is fire. He eats bushes, sheep, buckets, the hut, and finally the Mantis and Kwammang-a. The Porcupine burns her sons' ears with a hot spear to test who is fierce; the fierce ones cut the monster open, everything pours out alive, the world is set right, and the All-devourer utterly dies.
summary.zh: 為懲蜱人，螳螂召來全吞者——豪豬生父，舌如烈火。他食灌木、羊群、桶、屋，終吞螳螂與夸曼加。豪豬以熱矛燒其子之耳以試膽；勇者剖開巨怪，萬物盡出而復活，世界復原，全吞者遂滅。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San myth from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

narrative.en:
After the Ticks had beaten the Mantis and he had stolen their sheep, he wished for more: 'I want you, the Ichneumon, to catch some fat sheep, for father to cut up for us... The Man yonder shall come and eat with me of these sheep, because I have counted them and see they are plentiful.' The Porcupine warned him: 'Do you really want me to go to the Man who eats bushes? He will come and swallow all the sheep... we shall be swallowed with the sheep. A Man who devours things he is.'

She fetched her real father, the All-devourer. He followed her spoor, eating up the bushes as he came; his shadow glided over the Mantis's hut, and his red tongue was like a fire waxing. 'Is Father holding fire in his hand?' asked the Mantis. 'It is the Man coming there, whose tongue is red.'

The All-devourer arrived. The Mantis set meat before him, and the monster gulped it with the bushes it lay on. Buckets, water-bags, thorn-bushes, beds, the Porcupine's things — all vanished down the fire-tongue. The Mantis tried to hand him a bucket and his hands were scorched; he kept winking at the Dasse; the Ichneumon reminded him that no one invites this man. At last the All-devourer asked for 'the real food', burned the Mantis, and swallowed him — then Kwammang-a, with the bed he sat on. His stomach hung almost down to the earth.

The Porcupine reheated a spear and laid it burning on her younger son's temple, then in his nose: his tears gathered slowly, 'a mild person is this'. She laid it to the ear of young Kwammang-a, and his eyes stayed dry: 'Yes, a fierce man is this.' The children went out in wrath; each sat with spear arm outward, signed to one another, and cut the monster on both sides at once. They ran as their fathers poured forth — the sheep, the buckets, the pots, Kwammang-a on his bed. The All-devourer doubled up and died.

The children restored the world: 'O bushes, we have cut you out! You shall truly become bushes, you shall grow at your place... the place shall be right again and these sheep shall wander over it... that the people may get dry bushes and be able to warm themselves.' The young Mantis's speech came true. The Mantis himself drank a whole eggshell of water and fell; the Dasse beat his shin with a stick till he sat up. They moved away to a new home and left the monster lying before the old one, and lived in peace.

functions: World-renewal myth: the swallowed world is cut out and restored.
Charter for testing courage by endurance of burning.
Explains why the All-devourer-type being is never invited to share food.

variants.name: All-devourer's speech (B XXIII. 2161-2247)
variants.summary: The monster's speech to the Mantis and the Mantis's reply, recorded separately.

variants.name: Porcupine's warning version (L II.—32/33)
variants.summary: The connected version in which the Porcupine reluctantly fetches her father.

passages.text: The Porcupine said: 'Do you really want me to go to the Man who eats bushes? He will come and swallow all the sheep, as they stand in the kraal... A Man who devours things he is; he walks along eating up the bushes as he passes... The Mantis said to her: 'You must go to your other father, the All-devourer, that he may help me eat up these sheep, and drink this soup.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 34-35 (public domain).

passages.text: The All-devourer followed the Porcupine's spoor; as he went he ate up the bushes. He climbed up, finishing off the bushes, while his shadow glided up to the Mantis's hut. It fell upon the Mantis. The Mantis looked at the sun, he asked where the clouds were, for the sun seemed to be in clouds... 'Is Father holding fire in his hand, for a fire is waxing red yonder?' The Porcupine answered him: 'It is the Man coming there, whose tongue is red.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 35-36 (public domain).

passages.text: She heated the spear, she laid it burning hot to her son's ear-root; her son sat still. She heated the spear again, she said to her son: 'Remember, Grandfather's tongue is like this. You must sit firmly when you go to Grandfather.'... The All-devourer scorched the young Mantis's temple with his tongue... Young Kwammang-a looked hard at the other, he signed to him to hold his spear fast, and he held his own well.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 38-39 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: They ran away, while their fathers poured forth; the sheep also poured forth, the buckets poured forth; his father sat on the bed; the pots poured forth; the things poured down. His Grandfather doubled up and died. The children said: 'O bushes, we have cut you out! You shall truly become bushes, you shall grow at your place... the place shall be right again and these sheep shall wander over it... that the people may get dry bushes and be able to warm themselves.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 39-40 (public domain).
